# Packaging Principles

## Motion hierarchy

- One shot, one primary motion. Choose push, pull, lateral move, crash zoom, or hard-cut rhythm; do not stack all of them.
- Reserve the strongest motion for one opening, one climax, and one ending accent. A technique repeated on every shot loses emphasis.
- Match camera movement to subject movement. A leftward UI transition should move left; a person walking right should not be contradicted by a reverse push.
- End motion on a readable composition. After a fast move, hold long enough for the viewer to parse the subject.

## Rhythm

- Energy should rise and fall. Constant maximum energy reads as noise; constant low energy reads as a slideshow.
- Vary shot length intentionally. Use short shots for acceleration and longer shots for breathing, observation, or emotion.
- A hard cut is a valid transition. Use it more often than decorative wipes.
- A hold is part of the edit. Do not trim every clip immediately after its action resolves.

## Text and overlays

- Add text only when it carries a fact, title, instruction, label, or emphasis that the picture alone does not communicate.
- Keep one dominant text layer at a time. Avoid simultaneous title, caption, and badge competition.
- Respect safe areas and contrast. Add a scrim only when needed for legibility; do not cover the subject.
- Animate text with one readable entrance and a stable hold. Avoid looping or pulsing text unless it is the designated rhythm device.

## Transitions and effects

- A transition should explain a change: scene, chapter, location, time, or product state.
- Prefer 1-2 purposeful transitions per short video. Hard cuts should carry the rest.
- Effects should strengthen the subject, not hide it. Reject effects that blur faces, text, or important action.
- Use flash, shake, glitch, and heavy zoom sparingly. They are accents, not a baseline.

## Audio

- Dialogue is primary. Music and effects must duck below speech and return smoothly.
- Analyze music before placing beat-synced cuts. Do not fake a grid with evenly spaced guesses.
- Put music fades at the edit boundaries, not only at the beginning and end of the file.
- Sound and picture should peak together only for deliberate hits. Do not hit every beat.

## Verification

- Check the opening without context: can a new viewer tell what the video is about?
- Check the longest holds and the shortest cuts. Both should feel intentional.
- Check every overlay for safe-area clipping and contrast.
- Check the ending: it should resolve the energy rather than simply stop at the music boundary.
